cim: Faith in the Age of AI: How Religious Americans Are Using Artificial Intelligence
cim_eredeti: Faith in the Age of AI: How Religious Americans Are Using Artificial Intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has quickly become part of Americans’ everyday lives, even as many express concerns about its broader economic consequences. According to data from PRRI’s 2026 American Values Survey, two in ten Americans report using AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or Copilot at least once a day or more, although its use varies across demographic groups.[1] At the same time, most Americans believe the rapid expansion of AI will benefit big corporations while hurting American workers. While AI is increasingly used for a variety of purposes, its use in religious life remains relatively limited, with only one in ten Americans reporting they use AI for Bible study, prayer, spiritual guidance, or other religious purposes at least once a day or more. This Spotlight Analysis examines Americans’ views and use of artificial intelligence, including how frequently they use AI, who is most likely to use it, and the extent to which Americans are incorporating AI into their religious practice.

Most Americans report having used artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or Copilot (72%) over the past year, including more than four in ten who report using AI at least once a week. Among weekly AI users, two in ten use it once a day (8%) or several times a day (12%), while two in ten say they use AI once a week (8%) or multiple times a week (14%). Three in ten Americans say they have at least used AI a few times in the past year, including 10% who use it once or twice a month, 5% a few times a year, and 15% who seldom use it. About one-quarter of Americans (24%) say they have not used AI tools in the past year.

There are very few differences in AI use by party affiliation, with around two in ten Democrats (21%), independents (21%), and Republicans (20%) reporting using AI at least once a day.

Non-Christians (28%) and Black Protestants (27%) are the most likely to say they use AI at least once a day or more, compared with about two in ten members of all other religious groups. One in ten non-Christians (12%) say they never use AI, compared with one-quarter of all other religious traditions.

A slim majority of AAPI Americans (52%) say they use AI at least once a day, while 22% of Black, 18% of white, and 18% of Hispanic Americans report similar AI use frequency. By contrast, Hispanic Americans (26%), white (25%), and Black Americans (25%) are about three times as likely as AAPI Americans to report not using AI at all (8%).

Looking at Americans by age, Americans ages 65 and older are the least likely to use AI, with only 10% reporting they use it at least once a day, compared with about one in four Americans ages 18-29 (21%), ages 30-49 (26%), and ages 50-64 (23%). Four in ten Americans 65 and older (40%) say they never use AI, followed by 27% of those ages 50-64, 17% ages 30-49, and 16% ages 18-29. Americans with a four-year degree or higher are more likely than those without a four-year degree to say they use AI at least once a week; men are also more likely than women to use AI at least once a week.

One in ten Americans report using AI at least once a day for religious purposes such as Bible study, prayer, or spiritual guidance (10%), with another one in ten using it at least once a week (10%). Another two in ten say they use it once or twice a month, a few times a year, or seldom for religious purposes, and a solid majority of Americans (57%) say they never use AI for religious purposes. Similar to general AI usage, there are little differences by partisan groups, with one in ten Republicans (11%), independents (10%), and Democrats (9%) saying they use AI for spiritual purposes at least once a week.

Two in ten non-Christians (20%) say they use AI for spiritual purposes at least once a day, followed by 14% of Black Protestants and less than one in ten white mainline/non-evangelical Protestants (9%), white evangelical Protestants (8%), Hispanic Catholics (8%), unaffiliated Americans (7%), and white Catholics (6%). By contrast, non-Christians (51%) and Black Protestants (44%) are the least likely to report they never use AI for spiritual purposes compared with about six in ten members of all other religious groups.

AAPI Americans (17%) are more likely than white and Hispanic Americans (8% each) to report using AI for spiritual purposes at least once a day; about one in ten Black Americans (12%) also report daily use. Unlike general AI use, there are no significant differences in frequency of AI use for religious purposes by age, education, and gender.

When comparing AI use to more traditional forms of religious practice, Americans are significantly more likely to pray (35%) or read religious texts (14%) than use AI for religious purposes (10%) once a day or more. This pattern holds true for white evangelical Protestants and Black Protestants, with more than six in ten (65% and 62%) praying and one-third reading religious texts (32% and 31%, respectively) daily, compared with about one in ten (8% and 14%, respectively) using AI for spiritual purposes. Hispanic Catholics, white Catholics, and white mainline/non-evangelical Protestants are more likely to report praying at least once a day than to use AI for religious purposes, however, they are just as likely to say they read religious texts as they are to say they use AI for spiritual purposes. Interestingly, non-Christians are less likely to read religious texts once a day or more (12%) but are not significantly different in their frequency of daily prayer (27%) or spiritual AI use (20%).

[1] The survey was conducted among a representative sample of 5,200 adults (age 18 and up) living in all 50 states in the United States, who are part of Ipsos’s KnowledgePanel, and an additional 339 who were recruited by Ipsos using opt-in survey panels to increase the sample sizes in smaller states. Interviews were conducted online between August 20 and September 7, 2026. The margin of error for the national survey is +/- 1.6 percentage points at the 95% level of confidence, including the design effect for the survey of 1.48. Additional information about the KnowledgePanel is available on the Ipsos website: ipsos.com/en-us/solution/knowledgepanel.
